title: Task-Context Alignment & The Router
subtitle: No strategy wins everywhere — build the router that sends each question class to its cheapest CORRECT arm, from your own graded grid
topics: Task-context alignment — matching technique to task shape, not to fashion
Reading your own grid — cheapest-correct per question class, not per average
The route-only-among-correct rule — a FAILED arm is ineligible at any price
The router's honest cost — classification overhead and the fallback path
Competency built: MEASURE + STRATEGIES (outcomes 6 and 2 of 6)

analogy.title: The Hospital Triage Desk
analogy.text: A hospital doesn't send every patient to the cheapest department, and it doesn't send everyone to the best-equipped one either — the triage nurse routes each case to the unit that can treat THAT case, and a unit currently failing its safety audit takes no patients at all, however short its queue. MedFlow's router is the triage desk for questions: threshold questions go to the tiny canonical-file unit, aggregations to the sub-agent ward, and any arm that failed its correctness audit on a question class is simply off the board for that class until it passes again.

antiPatterns: Routing to the cheapest arm by average — averages hide per-class failures; compressed averages 231 tokens AND fails Q9
Letting a FAILED arm stay routable because 'it usually passes' — the router's contract is correctness first, price second
A router with no fallback — when classification is unsure, degrade to the control arm, never to a guess

sections.title: Alignment Before Optimization
sections.body: Anthropic's long-horizon guidance ends in an alignment table: compaction fits extended back-and-forth, note-taking fits milestone iteration, sub-agents fit parallel research (canon: ANTHROPIC-CE). The generalization is this module's thesis: every context strategy has a task shape it serves, and applying it elsewhere costs you. Your own grid proves it. okf is unbeatable on canonical questions (Q3: 186 tokens) but it's a policy reader — it can't summarize Rosa Delgado's history. isolated costs 1,805 median on single questions — the sub-agent's clean window is priced into the tool layer — yet it's the right unit for aggregation work. compressed is brilliant until the abstraction step drops PA-1004 on Q9. The knowledge-graph course measured the same law on codebases: forced-graph won structural questions and lost comprehension ones. No arm wins everywhere. That is the finding, not the obstacle.

sections.title: The Router, Derived From Evidence
sections.body:
MedFlow's routed mode is a classifier plus a routing table — and the table is not designed, it is read off the graded grid: for each question class, the cheapest arm whose correctness on that class is 100%. From the shipped grid: structural/canonical → okf or graph; abstention → okf (a 157-token refusal); logic → compressed (passes Q5/Q6); aggregation → isolated (because compressed is disqualified there by its Q9 FAIL). Result: routed passes all 10 questions at a 239-token median vs naive's 1,696 — a 7.1x saving at 100% correctness, versus arms that saved more per call and forfeited it by failing (compressed at 231, savings void on Q9).

The rule that makes this defensible is the route-only-among-correct rule: a FAILED arm is ineligible for its failing class at ANY price. Q9's routed cell reads 1,796 tokens — expensive, because the honest table routes it to isolated. A router tuned on tokens alone would pick the 208-token FAIL and celebrate.

sections.title: What the Router Costs, Honestly
sections.body: Per the Honesty Rule, the router's own price tag: classification overhead (MedFlow's is a keyword classifier — near-free but fallible; an LLM classifier adds a call to every question), misclassification risk (a logic question routed to okf gets a threshold recital instead of reasoning — the fallback for low-confidence classification is the control arm, accepting naive's 1,696 tokens over a wrong-unit answer), and a second derived artifact: the routing table is derived from the grid, so U11's law applies — reroute after every re-measurement, or the router itself rots. These numbers are replay-mode (synthetic-pre-recording); the routing METHOD — cheapest-correct per class, re-derived from your own live grid — is the transferable asset, not the table.

sections.title: The Routing Table Is Data, Not Code

sections.question: Your compressed arm posts the best token number on aggregation questions (208 vs isolated's 1,796) but failed Q9 by dropping PA-1004. A stakeholder asks WHY the router 'wastes' 1,588 tokens per aggregation question. What is the correct defense?
options: A. The router is misconfigured; cheapest arm should win and Q9 was one bad run

B. Compressed's 208 tokens bought an answer missing a manual-review case — in a prior-auth system that's a clinician never seeing a pending request; the 1,588 tokens are the measured price of the complete answer, and an arm that failed the class is ineligible until it passes, at any price
C. Isolated should be replaced by naive, which also passes and reads more naturally
D. The grader is too strict; PA-1004 was only one fact among several correct ones
sections.explanation: Savings void: 208 tokens for a wrong answer isn't a saving, it's a discount on a defect. The route-only-among-correct rule prices completeness explicitly — and if compressed's fidelity assertion is later fixed and re-measured to 100% on aggregations, the table re-derivation admits it back automatically. (C fails on price: naive passes Q9 at 1,700, no better than isolated and worse elsewhere; D misreads grading — a dropped load-bearing fact is the failure class the grader exists for.)

sections.title: Routers That Rot or Lie
items: The average-cost router: picks arms by grid-wide medians and quietly serves compressed's Q9 failure — per-class verdicts are the routing unit, never averages.
The frozen table: grid re-measured after a seed or model change, routing table not re-derived — the router now optimizes for a world that no longer exists (U11's law, applied to itself).
The guessing fallback: classifier unsure, router picks its favorite arm anyway — the only safe fallback is the control arm you've already graded everywhere.

takeaway: No context strategy wins every task, so stop looking for one: derive a routing table from your own graded grid — cheapest arm per question class among those at 100% correctness — and re-derive it whenever the grid changes, because a router is itself a derived fact.
labUnderstand: Ask one question from each class in routed mode and read which arm the receipt says served it (routed:okf, routed:isolated…), then verify each choice against the grid: cheapest-correct per class, including the Q9 case where the cheap arm was disqualified.
labBuild: With Claude, build derive_routes.py from the code section, run it on replay-fullgrid.json, and prove the rule twice: it must route aggregation AWAY from compressed (FAIL) — then flip Q9-compressed's fixture to a correct answer, re-grade, re-derive, and watch compressed become eligible again.
